title: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT

videos.script: Three lessons of design, and now you ask it something. SELECT is the statement you will write more than everything else in this course put together. {{select}} It looks simple, and it is, and there is exactly one thing about it that explains almost every confusing error message you will get in the next year. So we do that first. {{one-thing}} You write the clauses in one order — SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY. The database runs them in a different one. It starts with FROM, because it has to know which rows exist before it can throw any away. Then WHERE. Then, and only then, SELECT. {{order}} That is why naming a column in SELECT and using that name in WHERE does not work. When WHERE runs, the name you invented does not exist yet. Nobody tells you this, and the error message does not say it either. {{why}} The other half of this lesson is the two things that decide what a person actually sees: the order rows come back in, and how many. {{last-two}} Both are places where the obvious answer is wrong at scale. A query with LIMIT and no ORDER BY does not have a stable answer. And OFFSET, which is how everybody writes paging, gets slower the further in you go — and can show somebody the same row twice while they are reading. {{paging}}
